beats.beat: Walter speaks the household's true name three times on the open deck, as the letter instructs.
The lock answers, drawing a visible chill through his hand as it clicks open, his fingers going numb and pale.
Inside is not finished medicine but his grandmother's own formulary, water-stained, and a wrapped lump of raw fissure stone matching the lock.
Trying afterward to say his family name aloud for the record, Walter finds the word will not come; the lock has taken the name itself as payment.
Maud recognizes the wrapped stone as the same material salvagers now pull from near the fissure, meaning the grandmother's remedy was tested against the very substance still turning up today.

turn.note: Maud's closing line ties the recovered formulary to stone still being salvaged today, setting up a test of the remedy against the present-day substance.

trope_note: The cursed object pays off straight here (the lock's exact, stated price), and what the old world knew lands cleanly through the formulary and matching stone; no fourth trope introduced.
fixes: Trim slightly for length: 'He opened and closed them, and they came back slowly, and not all the way.' can lose its final clause without losing the image.
Consider cutting the repeated cold imagery across 'Then the cold came up out of it...' and the following sentence about candle-wax fingers; one is enough.
